title: Design a News Feed / Timeline (like Twitter/Instagram): fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read, celebrity problem, ranking algorithm, pagination, caching feeds.
shortTitle: Design a News Feed / Timeline (like Twitter/Instagram)
keyPoints: Fan-out-on-write pushes new posts into every follower's precomputed feed for fast reads (the common case).
Fan-out-on-read assembles the feed on demand by pulling from followed accounts (cheap writes, slow reads).
The celebrity problem breaks pure fan-out-on-write: millions of writes for one post from a mega-account.
Hybrid approach: fan-out-on-write for normal accounts, pull-on-read for celebrities, merged at read time.
Ranking replaces pure chronological order with a score combining recency, engagement, and affinity.
Cursor-based pagination is stable when new posts arrive; offset-based pagination causes duplicates or gaps.
Accept eventual consistency for feeds: a feed being a few seconds stale harms nobody, unlike a bank balance.

s1_definition.oneliner: Push posts into follower feeds at write time for fast reads, pull on read for celebrities, rank instead of pure time order, and cache feeds with cursor pagination.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fan-out-on-write** : when someone posts, immediately write the post id into every follower's precomputed feed list.
- **Fan-out-on-read** : assemble the feed on demand by pulling recent posts from everyone the user follows.
- **Celebrity problem** : a user with millions of followers makes fan-out-on-write prohibitively expensive.
- **Hybrid** : fan-out-on-write for normal accounts, pull-on-read for celebrities, merged at read time.
- **Cursor pagination** : use the last-seen post id or score as the cursor, stable when new posts arrive.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has an in-app feed where Rajesh sees updates from advisors and channels he follows. Two ways to build it: push every post into each follower's inbox (fan-out-on-write) or gather posts when Rajesh opens the app (fan-out-on-read). The first is fast to read but heavy to write; the second is the opposite. Real banks blend both.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  News Feed Architecture

  Post creation:
  ┌──────────┐  new post  ┌──────────────┐
  │  Author  │───────────►│  Post Store  │
  └──────────┘            └──────┬───────┘
                                 │
                    ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                    │ normal     │            │ celebrity
                    │ account    │            │ account
                    ▼            │            │
          ┌──────────────┐      │     (no fan-out,
          │ Fan-out to   │      │      pull on read)
          │ each follower│      │
          │ feed (Redis) │      │
          └──────────────┘      │
                                │
  Feed read:
  ┌──────────┐  open feed  ┌────▼───────────┐
  │  Reader  │────────────►│ Precomputed    │
  │          │             │ feed (Redis)   │
  │          │◄────────────│ + celebrity    │
  │          │  ranked,    │ posts (pulled) │
  │          │  paginated  │ + ranked       │
  └──────────┘             └────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A news feed system builds a personalized list of posts for each user. The central decision is between fan-out-on-write (fast reads, heavy writes) and fan-out-on-read (cheap writes, slow reads). The celebrity problem breaks pure fan-out-on-write, so the mature solution is a hybrid: fan-out for normal accounts, pull for celebrities, merged at read time.

Ranking replaces pure chronological order, cursor pagination keeps pages stable, and I accept eventual consistency because a stale feed harms nobody.

At National Bank of India, this powered an in-app feed where advisors' tips were fanned out but official announcements from the mega-channel were pulled on read.

Remember one sentence: fan out on write for normal accounts, pull on read for celebrities, rank for relevance, paginate with cursors, and accept eventual consistency for feeds.
